articles.title: Counts, sums, averages, minimums, and maximums
articles.summary: Count related records and calculate correctly scoped totals.
articles.body:
Summarize the records that are actually available to the template. Filtering a query changes the input to the total.

**Before you start:** Choose the fields and relationships in [Choose information](#choose-data). For an orientation and the format checklist, open [Find the right merge tag](#merge-tags).

#### Aggregates

Grand totals across a child relationship. Works in sync and giant-query paths.

```
{COUNT:OpportunityLineItems}                          1000
{COUNT:OpportunityLineItems:number}                   1,000
{SUM:OpportunityLineItems.TotalPrice}                 50000
{SUM:OpportunityLineItems.TotalPrice:currency}        $50,000.00
{SUM:Lines.Amount:currency:EUR:de_DE}                 50.000,00 €
{AVG:OrderItems.UnitPrice:currency}                   $127.50
{MIN:Quotes.Amount:currency}                          $100.00
{MAX:Deals.Amount:currency:GBP}                       £999,999.00
{SUM:Lines.Amount:currency:auto=CustomerCurrency__c}  uses the parent record's currency
```

All five functions support any format suffix (`currency`, `number`, `percent`, custom patterns), including `currency:auto` (see [Auto-detecting the currency from the record](#auto-detecting-the-currency-from-the-record)).

**Aggregate fields don't need to be rendered columns** — you can aggregate `UnitPrice` even if your loop table only shows `Product2.Name` and `Quantity`. The resolver validates field names against the child object's schema.

articles.title: Charts and every chart modifier
articles.summary: Choose chart types, data sources, styling, labels, and rendering paths.
articles.body:
Start with a one-line chart, then add only the options you need. Chart rendering depends on the output format and the way the document is generated; use the matrix below before building a large report. **Before you start:** Choose the fields and relationships in [Choose information](#choose-data). For an orientation and the format checklist, open [Find the right merge tag](#merge-tags). #### Charts Render **nine chart styles** inline in your generated documents — bar, column, pie, donut, pivot, stacked, clustered, line, and area. Charts use a prepared PNG image on supported paths, with browser rendering for interactive work and an Apex rasterizer for server work. HTML can also use CSS chart blocks or opt-in browser-only SVG. Excel output does not embed chart-tag images. Test the exact entry point you intend to use: | Output | How charts get there | | ------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | | HTML → browser | `` | | HTML → PDF | Same `` — Flying Saucer (`Blob.toPdf`) fetches it server-side | | Word `.docx` | `` referencing a PNG embedded in `word/media/` | | Word → PDF | Word → HTML → PDF chain; the embedded PNG flows through transparently | | PowerPoint `.pptx` | `` referencing a PNG in `ppt/media/` | | Excel `.xlsx` | (Coming in a follow-up release) | **Zero external callouts.** The chart engine is 100% native Apex — same constraint that makes Portwood suitable for AppExchange security review and managed-package customers. Charts work in Flow actions, batch jobs, Queueables, and Apex tests as well as the runner LWC. **Two authoring paths:** 1. **`{Chart:relationship:field:style:opts}`** — one-line tag. The engine resolves bucket data via SOQL aggregate (constant cost regardless of row count), rasterizes to PNG, embeds the image. Works on supported Word, HTML/PDF, Canvas, and PowerPoint paths; Excel image embedding is not supported. **This is the canonical path — use it for 95% of cases.** 2. **`{#ChartBucket:relationship:field}…{/ChartBucket}`** — hand-authored loop. You write the chart HTML body yourself with `{key}` / `{count}` / `{percent}` placeholders. Use only when you need a custom layout the engine doesn't ship (e.g., embedded sparklines inside a table cell). #### One-line `{Chart:...}` blocks A single tag that expands into a complete chart image at render time. **Tag syntax:** ``` {Chart:RELATIONSHIP:FIELD:STYLE:OPTS} ``` | Position | Required | Meaning | | -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | | `RELATIONSHIP` | yes | Child relationship name on the parent record (one-hop) | | `FIELD` | yes | Field on the child to group by | | `STYLE` | no | One of nine styles (default: `bar`) | | `OPTS` | no | `key=value&key=value` modifiers | **All nine styles:** | Style | Visual | Cross-tab? | Best for | | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | | `bar` | Horizontal bar per bucket, label left, count+% right | no | One question, one dimension. Long category labels. | | `column` | Vertical bar per bucket, labels under, % above | no | One question, one dimension. Short labels. | | `pie` | Pie chart with right-side legend showing count + % | no | "Share of total" framing, ≤8 slices | | `donut` | Pie with a center hole, same legend | no | Same as pie, lighter visual weight | | `pivot` | Cross-tab table — rows = buckets, cols = `groupBy` values + Total | required | Numeric matrix readout. CSS-bar path (HTML-friendly). | | `stacked` | Horizontal stacked bar — one row per bucket, segments by `groupBy` | required | "How does each row break down across the 2nd dimension?" | | `clustered` | Vertical clustered bars — one cluster per bucket, mini-bar per col | required | Side-by-side comparison across the 2nd dimension | | `line` | Polyline through (bucket index, count). Multi-series when `groupBy` present. | optional | Trend / ordering matters. Single or multi-series. | | `area` | Line chart with semi-transparent fill below each series | optional | Trend + accumulated volume | **Worked examples** (against the canonical Commute Survey Demo — 425 responses, 6 modes, 2 locations): ``` {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:bar:title=Commute Mode Distribution} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:column:title=Commute Mode (Vertical)} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:pie:title=Commute Mode Share} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:donut:title=Commute Mode Share (Donut)} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:stacked:groupBy=Location__c&colSort=8000 Marina,3260 Bayshore&title=Location Mix per Mode} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:clustered:groupBy=Location__c&colSort=8000 Marina,3260 Bayshore&title=Mode by Location Comparison} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:line:groupBy=Location__c&colSort=8000 Marina,3260 Bayshore&title=Commute Trend by Location} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:area:groupBy=Location__c&colSort=8000 Marina,3260 Bayshore&title=Commute Volume by Location} {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:pivot:groupBy=Location__c&colSort=8000 Marina,3260 Bayshore&title=Mode by Location (Table)} ``` #### Complete modifier reference Modifiers come after the style, joined with `&`. **Order doesn't matter.** Values containing `&` or `=` are not supported (use `where=` for SOQL with operators — see below). | Modifier | Applies to | Example | What it does | | ------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `title=` | all styles | `title=How satisfied are you with your role?` | Chart header text drawn above the chart. Becomes the `` attribute on the HTML side. | | `width=` | all styles | `width=420` | Logical-pixel width of the chart. Defaults: 540 (stacked/clustered), 500 (bar/column/line/area), 360 (pie/donut). Word/PDF downsample bigger PNGs for free AA. | | `height=` | all styles | `height=240` | Logical-pixel height. Defaults vary per style (see source); bar auto-grows by bucket count. | | `fontSize=` | all styles | `fontSize=16` | Axis-label size in pixels. Default 12; titles and other text scale with it, keeping their proportions. Raise it when the chart lands in a small frame. On a Canvas chart use the **Label size** box rather than writing the tag. Honoured by all three renderers — browser, Word/PowerPoint, and HTML-to-PDF. (v3.56+) | | `where=` | all styles | `where=Survey_Question__r.Display_Order__c=1` | SOQL fragment appended to the chart's `WHERE`. Identifier-only, sanitized through the same keyword blocklist as Query Builder. Forces server-side aggregation. | | `groupBy=` | stacked/clustered/pivot/line/area | `groupBy=Department__c` | Cross-tab dimension. **Required** for `stacked`/`clustered`/`pivot`; **optional** for `line`/`area` (omit → single-series). Field on the same child object as `FIELD`. | | `colSort=` | stacked/clustered/pivot/line/area | `colSort=Engineering,Sales,Marketing,Support,Operations` | Author-controlled column ordering. Named values appear first in this order; remaining values alpha-sorted; synthetic `Total` always last (pivot path only). | | `colors=` | all styles | `colors=#1e40af,#b91c1c,#16a34a` | Override the default 8-color palette. Cycles by row/series index. Each color is `#hex` (6 chars). | | `split=` | all (bucket-shape only) | `split=;` | Multi-select delimiter. Each respondent's pick contributes to every value they selected. Percentages sum to >100% by design. | | `scale=` | all (raster path only) | `scale=2` | Supersample multiplier. Default 1 for stacked/clustered/line/area, 2 for bar/column/pie/donut. Larger = sharper PNG but slower; 4 is the practical ceiling. | | `htmlRender=` | HTML browser preview | `htmlRender=svg` | (HTML only, opt-in.) Inline ``. **Browser-only — Flying Saucer drops SVG**. Prepared PNG images work in browser and PDF; without image preparation, supported CSS chart styles are the fallback. | **Composability:** every modifier composes with every other modifier where it makes sense: ``` {Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Mode__c:stacked:groupBy=Location__c&colSort=Marina,Bayshore&colors=#1e40af,#b91c1c&where=CreatedDate=THIS_YEAR&title=Modes by Office, 2026} ``` **Inside a relationship loop**, the chart's relationship resolves against the iterating record: ```html {#Survey_Questions__r}

Q{Display_Order__c}: {Question_Text__c}

{Chart:Survey_Responses__r:Selected_Answer__c:bar} {/Survey_Questions__r} ``` Here `Survey_Question__c.Survey_Responses__r` is the child relationship from Question (not from the outer Survey). One chart per question, no `where=` needed. > **If chart labels come out too small, raise `fontSize=`.** Label sizes are in canvas > pixels, so how big they look in the finished document depends on how far the image is > scaled to fit its frame. > > On a **Canvas** template that is straightforward: the chart block renders at its own > size, so the 12px default prints at about 9pt whatever size the block is. Set **Label > size** in the chart properties to change it. > > On a **PowerPoint or Word** template the image is stretched to fit the shape you drew, > and `width=` does not change that — a chart squeezed into a 3-inch shape has small > labels however many pixels it was rendered at. Raising `width=` sharpens the picture > while making the text smaller relative to the frame, which is the opposite of what > most people expect. `fontSize=` is the knob: adjust it until it reads well at the size > the shape actually is. **Error handling.** Malformed tags render an inline error block in HTML output (red border, monospace tag dump) and a `[Chart error: …]` text placeholder in Word — you see the problem at first preview rather than chasing a silent miss. Errors include the original tag verbatim so you can diff it against a working sample. #### Output-format matrix — what flows where The chart engine can emit prepared PNGs, HTML CSS chart blocks, or opt-in browser-only inline SVG. The result depends on the calling path and whether chart images were prepared. The runner LWC, Flow actions, batch jobs, and the Apex `generate*` entry points all orchestrate chart preparation automatically — **you do not call `prepareChartImages` in your template; just write the tags.** | Template Type | Output | Image format | Engine path | | ------------- | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | HTML | HTML download | `` referencing CV URL | Browser fetches the CV via lightning subdomain | | HTML | PDF | `` referencing CV URL | Flying Saucer's `Blob.toPdf` fetches the CV server-side (relative URL — managed-package safe) | | HTML | Browser preview | `` (default) OR inline `` referencing CV URL | Chart block previews live via Chart.js; the tag renders like any other HTML chart | | Flow / batch | any of the above | PNG via pure-Apex rasterizer | `DocGenChartImageController.prepareChartImagesServerSide` — no browser canvas, no callouts | #### Charts on large datasets — client-side rendering (v3.55+) The pure-Apex rasterizer runs inside a synchronous transaction, and both the chart data and the rendered PNGs have to fit in a 6 MB Apex heap. On a record with thousands of child rows that is not a limit you can tune around — a PowerPoint or Excel template over a few thousand child records used to fail outright with _"too large for sync PowerPoint/Excel output"_. For PowerPoint and Excel, Portwood now takes the same route it has always taken for Word: **the browser does the work.** The runner pages the child records down in chunks, aggregates each page into buckets as it arrives, and renders the finished chart with **Chart.js** on a real `` before embedding the PNG. Nothing large is ever held in Apex at once, so the heap ceiling stops being the constraint — verified against 30,000 child records. You do not opt in and you do not change your tags. Write `{Chart:...}` exactly as documented above; the runner picks the path. What you should know: - **It needs a browser.** Flow, batch and Apex entry points still use the server-side rasterizer, which is why the heap guidance in [§14.8](https://github.com/Portwood-Global-Solutions/Portwood/blob/main/UserGuide.md#148-template--output-size-guidance) still applies to unattended generation. - **Non-groupable fields are refused with a message.** A Long Text Area cannot be used in a SOQL `GROUP BY`, and attempting it throws an uncatchable platform exception — so Portwood checks the field first and tells you, rather than letting the transaction die. Group by a Text, Picklist, Number, Date or Checkbox field instead. - **Charts still render on the Canvas artboard** while you design, using the same library. **Cleanup.** Each generated chart produces a transient `docgen_chart_*` ContentVersion. The runner cleans them up after the document downloads/saves. A daily orphan reaper (`DocGenChartCleanupSchedulable`) sweeps stragglers (failures or browser-closed-mid-flow). #### LLM authoring prompt — copy this to generate a template Paste the block below into Claude / GPT / Gemini with one substitution: `${MY_DATA_DESCRIPTION}` should describe your child relationship name, the dimension field you want bucketed, and (optionally) the cross-tab field plus its expected values. The LLM will produce a complete HTML template you can upload. ```text You are writing a Portwood HTML template that renders 8 chart styles using Portwood's {Chart:...} tag syntax. Portwood is a native Salesforce 2GP package; the template is a single HTML file uploaded as a ContentVersion against a DocGen_Template__c with Type__c='HTML'. Hard constraints (Flying Saucer PDF engine, CSS 2.1 + small CSS 3 subset): - Use //
for layout OR
with display:table/table-row/table-cell. - Do NOT use: flex, grid, gap, linear-gradient, calc(), CSS variables. Silently ignored. - Do NOT use by default. - Wrap @page in a

articles.title: Images, assets, codes, rich text, and backgrounds
articles.summary: Insert images, shared assets, barcodes, QR codes, and rich text.
articles.body:
These tags place visual content in your document. A working image URL or valid asset key is part of the input, just as a selected field is part of a text tag. **Before you start:** Choose the fields and relationships in [Choose information](#choose-data). For an orientation and the format checklist, open [Find the right merge tag](#merge-tags). #### Images **Option 1 — record-attached (easiest).** `{%Image:N}` renders the Nth oldest image attached to the current record. No ContentVersion ID field, no query-builder setup — drag a photo onto the record in Files and the tag picks it up. Filters to PNG/JPG/GIF/BMP/TIFF/SVG automatically (non-image attachments are skipped). ``` {%Image:1} First image attached to the record, natural size {%Image:1:200} Max 200px in either dimension (preserves aspect) {%Image:1:200x200} Explicit 200px × 200px {%Image:1:400x} 400px wide, auto height {%Image:1:x150} Auto width, 150px tall {%Image:2}, {%Image:3} Second, third, … attached image ``` Inside a `{#Relationship}` loop, `{%Image:N}` scopes to the iterating record's images — ideal for inspection reports, real estate listings, product catalogs. Out-of-range indexes render empty silently. **Option 2 — image field (advanced).** When you need to pick a specific image that isn't the Nth attachment, store the ContentVersion ID (starts with `068`) in a text field and reference it: ``` {%ImageField} Embed an image from a rich text field or Files {%LogoImage:200x100} Width × height in pixels (see §7.7.2 for sizing in PDF) ``` Handles multiple sources automatically: - Rich text HTML `` — decoded and embedded - Raw base64 strings (100+ chars) — decoded and embedded - ContentVersion IDs (18-char, starts with `068`) — looked up and fetched - Salesforce file URLs (`/sfc/servlet.shepherd/...`) — resolved to blob - HTTPS URLs — embedded as URL references for PDF rendering **PDF path (special behavior).** For ContentVersion IDs, the PDF pipeline skips blob loading entirely — it uses relative Salesforce URLs (`/sfc/servlet.shepherd/version/download/`) and `Blob.toPdf()` fetches them natively via the VF rendering engine. This is what enables unlimited images in PDFs without heap pressure. **Image size limits.** PDFs with attached images are limited to roughly **30MB of total image content** for reliable Save-to-Record. Above that threshold, the save operation will error out (Salesforce platform limits on the ContentVersion insert path). If you need to include more images than this threshold allows, use **Download** instead of Save-to-Record — downloads work at a higher ceiling because they don't go through the same save pipeline. A typical inspection report with 20–30 phone photos fits within the 30MB ceiling; 50+ high-resolution photos may need to be downloaded and attached manually. #### Shared assets (`{%asset:}`) Use a **shared asset** when the same image — a logo, a footer band, a letterhead — appears in many templates and you want to update it in one place. Instead of pasting the same image (or its file ID) into every template, you reference the asset by a short, stable key. When you upload a new version of the asset, **every template that uses its tag picks up the new image automatically** — no template edits. **Set one up** from the **Command Hub → Assets** tab: give the asset a friendly name (e.g. "Primary Footer"), choose its **tag key** (a short, human-readable handle such as `footer`, suggested from the name and checked for availability as you type), upload an image, and copy its merge tag. The key is **permanent** — renaming the asset later never changes the key, so templates keep working — and it is case-insensitive (`{%asset:Footer}` and `{%asset:footer}` are the same asset). **Finding assets in a growing library (v3.30+).** The Assets tab shows a **thumbnail preview** of each asset's current image, and a **search box** filters the list live by name, tag key, merge tag, or category. Assets can carry an optional free-text **Category** ("Logos", "Footers", "Backgrounds" — any label you like, set when creating the asset or later via the row's **Edit** action); once at least one asset is categorized, a **category dropdown** appears next to the search box, including an _Uncategorized_ bucket. Categories are purely organizational — they never affect how the merge tag resolves. ``` {%asset:footer} Latest version of the asset whose key is "footer" {%asset:companylogo} (any key you chose when creating the asset) {%asset:companylogo:200x100} Fixed 200×100 px {%asset:companylogo:600x} Fixed 600 px wide, height auto (keeps aspect) {%asset:companylogo:x80} Fixed 80 px tall, width auto ``` > **Assets in email templates (v3.32+):** the same `{%asset:}` tag works inside **signature email templates** (Command Hub → Email Templates) — there it resolves to the asset's **public image URL** instead of embedding the image, so you write and size your own markup: ``. This is the easiest way to host email images in Salesforce Files: reference any asset in your email HTML, and replacing the asset's image later updates every email automatically. Size suffixes are ignored in emails (use CSS); saving or previewing the template publishes the referenced assets so recipients' email clients can load them. See §10.14. A size token must contain an `x` (the width × height separator); a bare number with no `x` is ignored. **Pixels (`px`, or a bare number) and percentages (`50%x`) are the supported units** — see **§7.7.2** for exactly what works in HTML → PDF (and the named-unit / max-width limits to be aware of). - Resolves to the asset's **latest** uploaded version every time a document is generated, so an updated logo flows through to all referencing templates at once. - Works across **Word, HTML, PDF, and PowerPoint** output, in the document body and in headers/footers — including very large datasets. - **Cross-user by design:** an asset one administrator creates renders correctly in documents other users generate. - **Deactivate** an asset (rather than deleting it) to retire it without losing history. A tag that points at a deactivated or unknown key renders a small `[missing asset: ]` placeholder so you notice it in review — it never breaks document generation. **What the tag produces.** The tag resolves to the asset's current image and then flows through Portwood's normal image pipeline, so it behaves like an inline image native to each format. You place the tag **where you want the image to appear** — you do not wrap it in your own `` or pass it to a `src`; the tag _is_ the image. | Output | What `{%asset:key}` becomes | | ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **HTML / PDF (HTML template)** | An `` element. The relative URL is fetched at render — exactly what the PDF engine (Flying Saucer) needs; no absolute URLs or data URIs required. A size token on the tag (`:300x`, `:200x100`, `:50%x`) is honored precisely; with no token the image renders at its natural size (capped to `max-width:100%`). See **§7.7.2** for the supported units and limits. | | **Word (`.docx`)** | The image bytes are **embedded** directly in the document. The `.docx` is self-contained and shows the image offline. | | **PDF (Word template)** | Referenced by relative URL via the zero-heap path, so large images don't exhaust heap on big jobs. | | **PowerPoint (`.pptx`)** | Embedded as a picture shape on the slide. | | **Excel (`.xlsx`)** | Image assets are **not** rendered in Excel output in v1 — the tag is removed cleanly (no error). | | **Large datasets (>2000 rows)** | Tags in headers, footers, and grand-summary areas resolve the same way (the high-volume rendering path emits the same ``). | **Permissions:** administrators (Portwood Admin) create and manage assets; standard Portwood users get read-only access, which is all that is needed to generate documents that reference them. > **v1 scope:** shared assets are **images** only. Text/HTML snippet assets and pinning a template to a specific asset version are planned follow-ups. #### Sizing images in HTML → PDF The size token on any image tag — `{%Image:N:…}`, `{%ImageField:…}`, `{%asset:key:…}` — controls the rendered size in **HTML-template → PDF** output. (As of **v3.26** these are honored precisely; earlier versions could collapse every size of the same image to one.) The rules below are specific to the PDF engine (Flying Saucer); Word/DOCX output is more flexible because Word does its own layout. **Supported units: pixels and percent only.** | Token | Result | | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `:300x100` | 300 px wide × 100 px tall (exact — may stretch off-aspect) | | `:300x` | 300 px wide, height **auto** (keeps aspect) | | `:x100` | 100 px tall, width **auto** (keeps aspect) | | `:50%x` | 50% of the page content width, height auto | | `:300` (bare) | `{%Image:N}` only → 300 px wide; on `{%Field}`/`{%asset}` a bare number with no `x` is ignored | A blank side means **auto** (aspect-preserving): `{%LogoImage:100x}` is the same as 100 px wide with auto height. Pixels map to physical size at **96 DPI** (so `:96x` ≈ 1 inch wide, `:288x` ≈ 3 inches). **Named units are not parsed.** `in`, `pt`, `cm`, `mm`, `pc` (e.g. `:3inx`, `:x25mm`) are silently ignored and the image falls back to natural size. Convert to pixels at 96 DPI: | 1 in | 1 cm | 1 mm | 1 pt | 1 pc | | ----- | ------- | ------- | ------- | ----- | | 96 px | 37.8 px | 3.78 px | 1.33 px | 16 px | So `:3inx` → `:288x`, `:x25mm` → `:x95`. **`max-width` / `max-height` are _not_ honored in PDF.** Flying Saucer applies only an explicit `width`/`height` to these images — a CSS `max-width`, `max-height`, or a "max size" token is ignored and the image renders at its natural size. There is no "cap large, leave small alone" sizing in PDF. - **Fitting a row of mismatched logos** (partner firms upload very different dimensions): give them all a **uniform width**, `{%Firm__r.Logo__c:200x}`. Each renders 200 px wide with proportional height — small logos scale up, large scale down, none distorted. (Avoid a fixed `:200x80` box for logos — it stretches them off-aspect.) **Hand-authored `` tags (advanced).** If you write your own `` instead of a `{%}` tag, you control the CSS directly, but two caveats apply: 1. Only `width`/`height` take effect — `max-width` does not (same engine limit as above). 2. The renderer computes one rendered size **per image URL** and reuses it. If you reference the **same** file at two different sizes, both come out the same. Add a throwaway query parameter to make each distinct (`…/068…?n=1`, `…/068…?n=2`). Portwood's `{%}` tags do this automatically, so prefer the tag unless you specifically need raw markup. (A grid of _different_ logos — different files — isn't affected.) #### Barcodes & QR codes ``` {*OrderNumber} Code 128 barcode (default) {*TrackingId:code128} Explicit type {*SKU:code128:300x80} 300×80 px {*ProductCode:qr} QR code {*URL:qr:200} 200px QR code ``` Barcodes render in Word **and** HTML templates (HTML support added in v3.15) across PDF and DOCX output. Types supported: `code128`, `qr` — **only** those two. A typo'd or unsupported type (e.g. `{*SKU:code39}`) renders nothing, silently; leaving the type off defaults to Code 128. QR codes are generated natively in Salesforce with Level Q error correction and support values up to 600 characters. For printed or mailed documents, short URLs or tokens under 120 characters are recommended for 1 inch square QR codes. #### Rich text fields When a field value contains HTML (`

`, `

`, `
`, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``), Portwood preserves the formatting in the output — paragraphs, line breaks, bold/italic/underline, hyperlinks, and embedded images all carry through. Works in **Word templates** (DOCX or PDF output) and **HTML templates** (PDF output). PowerPoint strips HTML to plain text. **Inline images in rich text** (the kind you paste directly into a Rich Text Area field) render across all three target formats — Word→PDF, Word→DOCX, and HTML→PDF — when you generate from the runner on a record page. Behind the scenes Portwood handles three flavors of image source automatically: - **Lightning inline images** (`/servlet/rtaImage?...&refid=…`) — refids that resolve to a `ContentVersion` (068/069 prefix) are rewritten to relative `/sfc/servlet.shepherd/…` URLs. `0EM` Lightning ContentReference refids aren't queryable, so they keep their absolute `*.file.force.com` URL — works in authenticated server-side rendering, but not in environments that lack reach to the file subdomain. - **Inline data URIs** (``) — DOCX and Word→PDF embed them; HTML→PDF drops them (Flying Saucer's `Blob.toPdf` can't decode data URIs). - **Hosted Salesforce file URLs** (`/sfc/servlet.shepherd/...`) — pass through to all targets. A few caveats: - The **Generate Sample** button in the template builder doesn't render inline rich-text images — they show as broken placeholders. Test the real output via the runner instead. - For pixel-perfect images, use the `{%Image:N}` tag with an attached File rather than inline rich text — DOCX image quality is slightly lossy when sourced from rich-text inline images. - Inline-image rotation isn't preserved. Rotate the source before pasting. - **Pre-size images before pasting.** Lightning's rich text editor doesn't write `width=`/`height=`/`style=` to the HTML it stores — even when you drag-resize the image in the editor, the displayed size never makes it into the saved markup. (In Chrome, drag-resize is disabled outright; Firefox lets you drag but the resize still doesn't persist.) Portwood falls back to a 4-inch default for DOCX output and to natural pixel dimensions for PDF output, so a phone photo pasted at 4000×3000 will render correctly in DOCX but bleed off the page in PDF. The reliable fix is to **resize the image to your intended dimensions in an editor BEFORE pasting** — once it's in the rich text field, the size is locked to whatever the source pixels were. For pixel-precise sizing across both formats, prefer `{%Image:N}` with `:WxH` (§7.7). Plain multiline (long text, textarea) fields work too — newlines in the field value render as proper line breaks in the output across all three targets. No manual `
` needed. #### Watermarks / page backgrounds (PDF output) Two ways to add a full-page watermark or background image to your PDF output: **Option A: Upload via the template builder (recommended).** In the template editor, click the **Watermark / Background** tab and upload a pre-sized image. This bypasses Word's Watermark dialog entirely and gives you exact pixel-level control over the output. A **Watermark strength** control (Light 15% / Medium 30% / Strong 50% / Original) fades the image — the opacity is baked into the stored PNG because Flying Saucer has no CSS opacity, and Portwood keeps the unfaded original so changing the strength after upload re-fades from it rather than compounding. The new setting applies immediately and survives a page reload (v3.57+). **Option B: Insert via Word's Design → Watermark dialog.** Word's built-in watermark works too, with these constraints: - **Scale must be set to 100%.** Word's "Auto", "50%", etc. scale settings are ignored by the PDF renderer — only the source image's pixel dimensions matter. - **Washout must be OFF.** Leave the Washout checkbox unchecked. To get a faded look, pre-fade the image in an editor (~15–20% opacity over white) BEFORE inserting in Word. - **No rotation.** Word's 315° diagonal default isn't honored. If you need a rotated watermark, save the image pre-rotated as a PNG. Both options use the same rendering pipeline — `@page { background-image: url(...) }` extending edge-to-edge across the full page bleed. **Pre-resize your watermark image to the page dimensions at 96 DPI** (the resolution Flying Saucer renders at — NOT the standard 72 DPI you might assume from PDF specs): | Page size | Pixels at 96 DPI | | -------------------- | ----------------- | | Letter (8.5 × 11 in) | **816 × 1056 px** | | A4 (8.27 × 11.69 in) | **794 × 1123 px** | | Legal (8.5 × 14 in) | **816 × 1344 px** | Other limitations (apply to both options): - **Text watermarks** ("DRAFT", "CONFIDENTIAL" via Word's text watermark option) are not supported. Use a picture watermark with the text rendered into a PNG. - **DOCX output preserves whatever Word would render natively** — these constraints only apply to PDF output. #### Approved PDF font tags Use `{%font:asset-key:revision}` only inside a quoted inline `style` attribute, as a complete style declaration. Copy the real tag from the approved face in **Assets → Custom Fonts**; the revision pins the exact face instead of choosing a mutable latest font. ```html

Prepared for {Name}

``` Use one font tag per element. Do not write `font-family:{%font:…}` or combine it with another font-family/weight/style override; the tag supplies those declarations. You can add font size, color, and other non-font-face styling. The face must have passed native PDF review; a missing, ambiguous, or unapproved revision can fail validation. Test retired/deleted font dependencies before changing them. For page furniture, use [CSS page-counter spans](#running-headers-footers) rather than putting a font tag and literal page-number tokens in the same header/footer. This registry controls native PDF rendering, not a recipient's Office font installation. See [Upload and approve a custom font](#custom-fonts).

articles.title: Signature tags and variable signer blocks
articles.summary: Place signatures and initials, match roles, and repeat signer sections.
articles.body:
Signature tags reserve places for named signing roles. A role in the template must match the role supplied when you create the signing request.

**Before you start:** Choose the fields and relationships in [Choose information](#choose-data). For an orientation and the format checklist, open [Find the right merge tag](#merge-tags).

#### Signatures

See [§10](https://github.com/Portwood-Global-Solutions/Portwood/blob/main/UserGuide.md#10-e-signatures-v3) for the full signature feature. Tag syntax:

```
{@Signature_Buyer}                  v2 — typed full signature (default)
{@Signature_Buyer:1:Full}           v3 — role=Buyer, order=1, type=Full signature
{@Signature_Buyer:1:Initials}       v3 — initials
{@Signature_Buyer:1:Date}           v3 — auto-filled signed date
{@Signature_Buyer:1:DatePick}       v3 — user-chosen date
{@Signature_Loan_Officer:2:Full}    Role names with underscores for multi-word
{@Signature_Buyer:1:Full:inline}    v3 — compact in-place mark, no stamp card (tight layouts)
```

- **Role**: any string (Buyer, Seller, Witness, Loan_Officer, etc.). Underscores become spaces in the UI.
- **Order**: sequence number per-role (optional, defaults to 1). Used for sequential signing and multi-placement per signer.
- **Type**: `Full` | `Initials` | `Date` | `DatePick` (optional, defaults to `Full`).
- **Style** (optional): add `:inline` as a final suffix (e.g. `{@Signature_Buyer:1:Full:inline}`, `{@Signature_Buyer:1:Date:inline}`) to render a **compact in-place mark** instead of the stamp card. See [§10.7.2](https://github.com/Portwood-Global-Solutions/Portwood/blob/main/UserGuide.md#1072-stamp-card-vs-inline--how-a-signature-renders).

Pre-signing, tags are preserved in the output (not replaced). Post-signing, each tag position carries the signer's mark as a **stamp card** — drawn ink or typed name in a signature font, with a "Signed by X · date" caption (see §10.10). Date tags stamp the signed date as text.

#### Signature loop block — `{#Signatures}` (variable signer count)

Role tags above pin each signer to a **fixed spot** — perfect when you know the parties (Buyer + Seller). But when the **number of signers varies** (a quote signed by one person today, three next week), you'd otherwise need a separate template per count, and any unused role tag leaks as literal text.

The `{#Signatures}` loop block solves this: author **one** signature layout and it repeats **once per signer**, for any count, wherever you place it in the document.

```
{#Signatures}
  ______________________________
  {Name}
  Electronically signed on {SignedDate}
  {Role} · {Email}
{/Signatures}
```

Per-row fields available inside the block:

| Field              | Value                                                                                           |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `{Name}`           | The name the signer typed at signing (their e-signature); the invited name if none was captured |
| `{RegisteredName}` | The name the signer was invited under                                                           |
| `{Role}`           | The signer's role (defaults to `Signer`)                                                        |
| `{Email}`          | The signer's email                                                                              |
| `{SignedDate}`     | The date they signed (blank before signing)                                                     |
| `{Status}`         | `Pending` before signing, `Signed` after                                                        |

**Styling is yours.** The block is plain template content, so style `{Name}` however you like — a cursive web font for a handwritten look, a bordered box, a two-column table of signers, etc. (HTML templates have full CSS control within the Flying Saucer CSS 2.1 subset; Word templates can style the line too.)

Notes:

- **Backwards-compatible and additive.** Role tags (`{@Signature_Role}`) are unchanged and continue to work exactly as before — use them when you want signatures in fixed, scattered positions. A template **without** a `{#Signatures}` block renders identically to previous releases. You can even combine both in one template.
- **Where it applies.** The loop is populated by the snapshot/PDF-viewer signing flow (the flow that re-renders the document from a send-time data snapshot and attaches the completed PDF + certificate to the record). Before signing, the block previews the invited signers with a `Pending` status; on completion it shows each signer's typed signature and signed date.
- **Typed-name signatures** today (drawn-signature images are a planned future enhancement; the loop already supports per-row image fields for when that lands).

articles.title: Print classic approval history
articles.summary: Show approvers, decisions, comments, and approval dates.
articles.body:
Use this built-in relationship for classic Salesforce approval history. Check the output against a record with an actual approval submission.

**Before you start:** Choose the fields and relationships in [Choose information](#choose-data). For an orientation and the format checklist, open [Find the right merge tag](#merge-tags).

#### Classic Approvals related list — `{#Approvals}` (v1.92+)

Render the host record's Salesforce **Classic Approvals** process history (submission, every approval/rejection step) directly in a generated document. Common use cases: Purchase Orders showing every approver up the chain in the final PDF, NDAs stamped with each signatory's role + timestamp, change-management forms with the approval audit trail rendered alongside the form data.

**Opt-in via Query_Config\_\_c.** Add the standalone word `Approvals` somewhere in the template's Query_Config**c (case-insensitive, word-boundary — `MyApprovalsList**c`doesn't activate it). When Portwood sees the token, it queries`ProcessInstance`+`ProcessInstanceStep`for the host record and exposes the flattened step list as a child collection at the`Approvals` key.

Example Query_Config\_\_c entry:

```
Name, Status__c, Amount__c, Approvals
```

Example template body:

```
{#Approvals}
{ActorName} ({ActorTitle}) — {StepStatus} — {CreatedDate:MM/dd/yyyy h:mm a}
Comments: {Comments}

{/Approvals}
```

**Fields available inside the loop:**

| Field               | Source                                                                                                 |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `ActorName`         | `Step.Actor.Name` — who actually took the action                                                       |
| `ActorTitle`        | `Step.Actor.Title` — title on the User who acted                                                       |
| `ActorEmail`        | `Step.Actor.Email`                                                                                     |
| `OriginalActorName` | `Step.OriginalActor.Name` — useful when an approval was reassigned (delegated to)                      |
| `StepStatus`        | `Started`, `Approved`, `Rejected`, `Removed`, `NoResponse` — see Salesforce docs for the full list     |
| `Comments`          | Approver's comments (empty string when omitted)                                                        |
| `CreatedDate`       | When the step occurred — works with the standard `{CreatedDate:MM/dd/yyyy}` format specifiers (§7.2)   |
| `ProcessStatus`     | The parent `ProcessInstance.Status` — the overall outcome of the approval process this step belongs to |
| `SubmittedByName`   | Who originally submitted for approval (constant within one ProcessInstance)                            |
| `SubmittedByTitle`  | Submitter's User.Title                                                                                 |

**Sorting.** Steps are sorted earliest-first within each ProcessInstance, and ProcessInstances are sorted earliest-first. So a record that was submitted, rejected, then resubmitted and approved produces the steps in chronological order across both submissions.

**What's not included (yet).** Only steps that have been _acted on_ appear — pending approval items (`ProcessInstanceWorkitem`) are not in the list. If you need "still awaiting approver X", that's a separate query. Flow-based approval orchestration is a different object model and out of scope; this tag covers the Classic Approvals process only.

**Cost.** One extra SOQL query per generation when the token is present. Templates that don't reference `Approvals` in Query_Config\_\_c skip the query entirely — no overhead.

articles.summary: Use semantic headers, understand the engine limits, and test per-page repetition.

articles.title: Build rich headers and two-line page footers
articles.summary: Keep formatted page furniture while showing Page X of Y.
articles.body:
Use a simple page-number tag for a simple footer. Use CSS counters when you need page numbers alongside multiple formatted lines, logos, or other HTML. #### The simple footer In **Footer HTML**, enter: ```html Page {PageNumber} of {TotalPages} ``` In the current engine, literal `{PageNumber}` or `{TotalPages}` in a header/footer selects a text-based page-margin path. The engine converts that HTML to text, so separate lines, images, and rich formatting can flatten. That explains a footer that looks right in the editor but loses its layout in the PDF. #### The rich footer 1. Put these rules inside the main template body's ``. 2. Put the following HTML in the template's **Footer HTML** field. 3. Keep literal `{PageNumber}` and `{TotalPages}` out of that header/footer. 4. Save a new active version and generate a multi-page PDF. ```css .pw-page-number:before { content: counter(page); } .pw-total-pages:before { content: counter(pages); } ``` ```html
Page of
Northstar Bikes | 317-555-0142 | hello@example.com
``` Without the literal counter tags, Portwood uses a running HTML element for page furniture. The pseudo-elements supply the counters while keeping the HTML structure intact. The 3.60.0 lab verified both footer lines and the correct `Page 1 of 4` through `Page 4 of 4` values. #### Make room for it Set enough top/bottom margin for the actual logo, line height, and number of lines. Choose one owner for page size and margins. Imported `@page` rules, the designer's page setup, and header/footer controls can otherwise compete. Keep counters in page furniture. These are PDF layout counters, not record fields or row numbers. A packet assembled from separately rendered PDFs can retain numbering from each original document; test whether that meets your requirement for the final packet. #### When something still looks wrong | Symptom | Check | | ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Everything becomes one line | Remove literal page-number tags from that header/footer and use counter spans | | Footer overlaps the body | Increase the bottom margin and reduce oversized content | | Page number is blank | Keep the CSS in the main body stylesheet; verify exact class names and final PDF | | Custom font and literal counters fail | Use running HTML plus CSS counters and test the approved font specimen | | Header image is missing | Confirm image access and dimensions in the actual render path | This recipe adapts Dave's [two-line footer answer in Portwood Community](https://portwoodcommunity.slack.com/archives/C0B37JT11RA/p1792162191491549), checked against `wrapHtmlForPdf` and a real 3.60.0 PDF.

articles.title: Build grouped reports without broken table markup
articles.summary: Create one table per category and keep group totals and loop scope correct.
articles.body:
Use one dataset and `{#GroupBy}` when the categories can change. Use deliberately filtered query aliases when each section has a different data-selection rule. #### One table per stage Select Opportunities with `Name`, `StageName`, and `Amount`. Sort by `StageName` if you want groups in stage order. This HTML wraps a complete table in the group and keeps the row loop inside its cells: ```html
{#GroupBy Opportunities by StageName}

{GroupName}

Opportunity Amount
{#Opportunities}{Name} {Amount:currency}{/Opportunities}

Stage total: {SUM:Opportunities.Amount:currency}

{/GroupBy}

All stages: {SUM:Opportunities.Amount:currency}

``` Inside the group, the Opportunities relationship contains that group's members. Outside it, the total sees the whole available relationship. `{RowNumber}` restarts within each group's row loop. #### A different alias is not a filter Renaming `{#QuoteLineItems}` to `{#Purchase}` does not select purchase items. `Purchase` must exist in Query Config or the supplied data. Either configure two filtered aliases, use a prepared provider, or keep the real relationship and apply conditions to its rows. A conditional display does not automatically change an aggregate over the unfiltered relationship. #### Keep table HTML valid Do not place naked loop/IF text directly between ``, ``, and ``. Browsers can move that text outside the table before Portwood processes it. Keep row-loop markers in cells, and place group markers outside complete tables. After switching between visual editing and HTML, inspect the saved markup and preview again. #### Respect scope Within a Contact loop, `{Name}` means the Contact's Name. To print the root Account's Name, use a uniquely named root block such as `{~AccountHeading}{Name}{/AccountHeading}`. Root-scope blocks are unsupported inside giant-query loops; use a prepared layout/data structure for that case. Test zero, one, and several groups, blank category values, and long labels. Compare group totals with a trusted Salesforce report before sharing the document.

articles.title: Tune a demanding document
articles.summary: Choose the right execution path, reduce waste, and isolate layout or data failures.
articles.body:
Start with the smallest document that proves the business result. Add data, graphics, and styling in stages so you can tell which change creates a problem.

#### Pick the path for the job

| Job                                                  | Starting point                                               |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| One normal record, interactive download              | Record-page Runner                                           |
| Many parent records                                  | Bulk Generation or Generate Bulk Documents Flow action       |
| One parent with a very large child list              | Auto Giant Query / the supported giant-query path            |
| Computed or external data already prepared           | JSON data or `DocGenDataProvider`; own the access checks     |
| A PDF Blob for another process, without a saved File | Global `DocGenService.generatePdfBlob…`                      |
| A packet of Portwood-native PDF parts in Apex        | Global `DocGenPdfMerger`, within its supported PDF structure |

Giant-query generation is asynchronous once it crosses the engine's large-relationship threshold. Follow the returned job rather than expecting an immediate File Id. It is different from bulk generation across many parent records.

#### Make the data smaller before making the heap larger

Select only used fields, filter relationships, order them deliberately, and set justified limits. Avoid huge rich-text fields and full-resolution images when the document prints a small thumbnail. A query limit changes the document's data and totals; disclose intended truncation to the reader rather than quietly hiding rows.

Use standard retrieval when it fits. When you supply JSON or an Apex map, Portwood cannot know whether your code was allowed to retrieve each value; enforce sharing, object access, and field access in the caller/provider.

#### Work with transaction boundaries

Do not assume a rendering API can run synchronously from a trigger or after arbitrary DML. Queue the document work into a fresh transaction and test the exact Flow/Apex entry point. Bulk rendering, chart preparation, file saves, and merging all consume resources. A method accepting a list does not promise unlimited work in one transaction.

Keep durable job outcomes and retries in your own process. Avoid retrying after an uncertain success without checking for the existing File/request; duplicate retries can create duplicate documents or invitations.

#### Use the PDF engine's strengths

Use tables for aligned print layouts, fixed units for controlled dimensions, simple borders, and a supported font. The renderer follows a CSS 2.1/paged model; browser flex/grid layouts, shadows, rounded corners, and JavaScript are not a reliable PDF design foundation. Use a pre-rendered image when a visual effect cannot be represented by the print engine.

For precise Word conversion, fix table widths and AutoFit rather than repeatedly changing the PDF's margins. The [layout reference](https://github.com/Portwood-Global-Solutions/Portwood/blob/main/docs/reference/template-layout.md) includes the width traps and a constrained HTML-authoring prompt.

#### Diagnose one variable at a time

1. Confirm the template, active version, record, output type, and running user.
2. Reduce to one field and one related row.
3. Add the original query selection, then loops and totals.
4. Add images, then charts, then page furniture.
5. Reintroduce the failing data volume last.
6. Compare preview, record Runner, and the actual automation path; they can prepare assets differently.

For a release, keep small, empty, long-text, many-row, multi-page, and representative image cases. Inspect the final files, not only the designer preview. A screenshot captures a symptom; the template version, query, data shape, and execution path make it reproducible.

articles.title: Generate documents from your own Apex
articles.summary: Choose a global generation method, save or return a PDF, and use a fresh transaction.
articles.body:
Use `portwoodglobal.DocGenService` from subscriber Apex. Start with the method that matches the result your process needs.

#### Choose the method

| Result you need                           | Global method                                                                 | Result                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| A File on the source record               | `generateDocument(templateId, recordId)`                                      | `ContentDocumentId`                                        |
| An explicit compatible output type        | `generateDocument(templateId, recordId, outputFormatOverride)`                | `ContentDocumentId`                                        |
| A saved File with a chosen title          | `generateDocument(templateId, recordId, outputFormatOverride, documentTitle)` | `ContentDocumentId`                                        |
| A different attachment target             | Add `attachmentRecordId` as the fifth argument                                | `ContentDocumentId`; null target creates a standalone File |
| PDF bytes without a saved File            | `generatePdfBlob(templateId, recordId)`                                       | Map with `blob` and `title`                                |
| A saved File from an already prepared map | `generateDocumentFromData(templateId, recordId, data)`                        | `ContentDocumentId`                                        |
| PDF bytes from a prepared map             | `generatePdfBlobFromData(templateId, data)`                                   | Map with `blob` and `title`                                |
| Prepared data with record context         | `generatePdfBlobFromData(templateId, recordId, data)`                         | Map with `blob` and `title`                                |
| Prepared data, output type, and File save | `generateAndSaveFromData(templateId, recordId, data, outputFormatOverride)`   | `ContentDocumentId`                                        |

`generateAndSaveFromData` also accepts a fifth `documentTitle` and a sixth `fileAttachmentTarget`. The second argument remains required. Passing a null sixth argument creates a standalone File; use a Blob method if you want no File at all.

#### Generate after the business transaction

A trigger or Flow can change records and then queue the document work. The worker gets a fresh transaction. Rendering is subject to platform transaction rules; do not paste a synchronous PDF call directly into a trigger and assume it is supported there.

The downloadable [KBGenerateAccountBrief class](https://github.com/Portwood-Global-Solutions/Portwood/blob/main/docs/knowledgebase/examples/apex/KBGenerateAccountBrief.cls) was deployed and executed in the fresh subscriber org. It looks up the template by its stable API Name and calls the global generation service from a Queueable implementing `Database.AllowsCallouts`.

```apex
// Run in your process after deciding this Account needs a document.
System.enqueueJob(new KBGenerateAccountBrief(accountId));
```

The example uses `KB_Account_Brief`, the [worked example](#example-library). Replace that stable key with your own template API Name. For a real deployment, add job outcome reporting, retries with duplicate protection, access checks appropriate to the caller, and tests for the business trigger.

#### Return bytes to another process

```apex
Map<String, Object> result = portwoodglobal.DocGenService.generatePdfBlob(templateId, accountId);
Blob pdf = (Blob) result.get('blob');
String title = (String) result.get('title');
// Your code can attach the bytes to an email or pass them to another system.
// This Portwood method does not itself send an email or create a File.
```

Read all inputs before rendering; keep preceding DML out of the render transaction. Test the exact document, image, and chart path you will use. Large outputs still consume Apex heap even when you do not save a File.

#### Handle access and failures deliberately

The standard retrieval path uses user-mode queries. A prepared map skips the source-record retrieval; template, file, font, and other supporting queries can still consume SOQL budget. Prepared maps and custom providers bypass that retrieval, so caller code must enforce access on the data it supplies. `with sharing` alone does not enforce field access.

Catch `portwoodglobal.DocGenException` for Portwood validation failures, and handle other platform/transaction failures in your job framework. Log safe identifiers and the failure reason; do not write entire documents, signing URLs, or sensitive merged values into logs.

The package's `DocGenController` and `DocGenBulkController` are internal UI controllers, not exported subscriber APIs. `@AuraEnabled` does not make a public controller global. Call the exported service/actions or your own authorized wrapper.

articles.title: Use PDF, email, and cleanup helpers
articles.summary: Understand the exported utility APIs and their practical limits.
articles.body:
These global helpers support specific jobs. Read the input limits before putting one into your process.

#### Merge Portwood-native PDFs

```apex
Blob packet = portwoodglobal.DocGenPdfMerger.mergePdfs(
    new List<Blob>{firstPdf, secondPdf}, true);
Integer pages = portwoodglobal.DocGenPdfMerger.pageCount(packet);
```

`mergePdfCvs(List<Id>, Boolean)` accepts ContentVersion Ids and loads parts incrementally. Passing `true` adds a blank page after every odd-length part, including the last part. Two one-page parts therefore produce four pages. The blank pages carry no page number; the content pages retain numbering baked into their original render.

This is a specialized server merger for Portwood's Flying Saucer/iText PDF 1.4 output with classic cross-reference tables and the expected page structure. It is not a general library for arbitrary uploaded product sheets, encrypted PDFs, object streams, or every PDF producer. Catch `DocGenPdfMerger.DocGenPdfMergeException` and use a compatible workflow for unsupported inputs. The packaged browser-side packet workflow is separate.

The 3.60.0 subscriber check generated a one-page Account Brief, merged two copies with padding, and confirmed the resulting four-page count.

#### Render a branded email without sending it

```apex
Map<String, String> tokens = new Map<String, String>{
    'SignerName' => 'Jordan Rivera', 'DocumentTitle' => 'Practice document',
    'SignatureUrl' => 'https://example.com/practice'
};
portwoodglobal.DocGenEmailTemplateService.RenderedEmail email =
    portwoodglobal.DocGenEmailTemplateService.render(
        portwoodglobal.DocGenEmailTemplateService.TYPE_REQUEST, tokens);
String subject = email.subject;
String html = email.htmlBody;
String plainText = email.plainBody;
```

Overloads add `messageOverride`, then `brandId`. `renderSubject(String, Map<String,String>)` resolves subject tokens. Rendering does not send an email, create a request, or authorize a signing URL. Use the appropriate email type/token contract and a real request's URL when building an actual notification.

The rendered subject and body were checked in the fresh org. No email was sent by this rendering test.

#### Schedule transient chart/PDF-part cleanup

```apex
System.schedule('Portwood transient cleanup', '0 0 * * * ?',
    new portwoodglobal.DocGenChartCvReaper());
```

Inspect Scheduled Jobs first so you do not add duplicate schedules. `reap()` is also exported and returns the number cleaned. The current helper targets old, orphan transient `chart_`/`pdfpart_` files, with age/job-state checks and a bounded batch. It is not a general Salesforce Files retention policy.

`DocGenEmailTemplateInstall` is the package install handler; `seedDefaults()` is an exported setup utility. Normal document generation does not require calling the install handler yourself.

#### Add native AI authoring

`DocGenAiProvider` requires `isAvailable()`, `getName()`, and `generateHtml(String)`. The optional Agentforce extension exports `DocGenEinsteinProvider`. Use [Agentforce setup](https://github.com/Portwood-Global-Solutions/Portwood/blob/main/docs/AGENTFORCE_SETUP.md) for entitlement and configuration. The native provider contract uses Einstein/ConnectApi and explicitly excludes HTTP-callout providers. Return a complete HTML document and handle unavailable configuration through `isAvailable()`.
